# Case Study 4: Gender Gap in Scientific Publishing

## Objective

Examine why a name lookup cannot establish a gender gap, using an explicitly
synthetic example of two fictional journals. We compare arbitrary lookup
categories, retain unmatched records in every denominator, and track lookup
coverage by recorded authorship position and year. None of the records represents
a real person, paper or journal; no gender identity is observed or inferred.

An actual study of gender equity requires a defensible demographic variable and
its provenance, a defined population, appropriate data governance, and a plan
for validation and missing data. A list of names is not a substitute for those
observations. Chapter \@ref(gender-objectives) develops these distinctions.

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: cs04-setup
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(glue)
library(gt)

source(here::here("R", "sci_palette.R"))
```

## Synthetic teaching records

The six invented papers have explicit publication years and ordered name lists.
The names are placeholders, and repeated names do not establish shared author
identity. Each row created below is an authorship record, not a distinct person.
This example makes no API request.

```{r}
#| label: cs04-synthetic-records
works_example <- tibble(
  work_id = c("example-a1", "example-a2", "example-a3",
              "example-b1", "example-b2", "example-b3"),
  journal = rep(c("Example journal A", "Example journal B"), each = 3),
  year = rep(2019:2021, 2),
  first_names = list(c("aria", "jordan", "lee"), c("noor", "ari"), "morgan",
                     c("aria", "nuri", "sam", "alex"), c("ari", "noor"),
                     c("lee", "jordan", "morgan"))
)
```

## Arbitrary lookup and complete denominators

For teaching purposes only, assign `aria` and `ari` to A, and `jordan` and
`morgan` to B. These arbitrary categories have **no demographic meaning**.
Every other name is explicitly unmatched. Dropping unmatched records would
change both the denominator and the question answered by a proportion.

```{r}
#| label: cs04-name-lookup
authors_example <- works_example |>
  unnest_longer(first_names, values_to = "first_name", indices_to = "author_order") |>
  group_by(work_id) |>
  mutate(
    n_authors = n(),
    position = case_when(
      n_authors == 1 ~ "single",
      author_order == 1 ~ "first",
      author_order == n_authors ~ "last",
      TRUE ~ "middle"
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    lookup_category = case_when(
      first_name %in% c("aria", "ari") ~ "A",
      first_name %in% c("jordan", "morgan") ~ "B",
      TRUE ~ "Unmatched"
    ),
    lookup_category = factor(lookup_category, levels = c("A", "B", "Unmatched")),
    position = factor(position, levels = c("first", "middle", "last", "single"))
  )

coverage_summary <- authors_example |>
  group_by(journal) |>
  summarise(records = n(), matched = sum(lookup_category != "Unmatched"),
            coverage = matched / records, .groups = "drop")
coverage_summary |> gt() |> fmt_percent(columns = coverage, decimals = 1)
```

## Lookup categories by fictional journal

```{r}
#| label: cs04-fig-cs04-journal
#| fig-cap: "Arbitrary lookup categories among all synthetic authorship records in two fictional journals; these are not gender proportions."
#| fig-alt: "Grouped bars show A, B and Unmatched shares using every synthetic record in each fictional journal as the denominator."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5
journal_summary <- authors_example |>
  count(journal, lookup_category, .drop = FALSE) |>
  group_by(journal) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(journal_summary, aes(x = journal, y = pct, fill = lookup_category)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = palette_sci(3), drop = FALSE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of all synthetic records", fill = "Lookup category") +
  theme_sci()
```

## Recorded authorship position

Single-author papers receive their own position label. In a real corpus,
recorded order does not by itself establish seniority or contribution: the
interpretation depends on authorship conventions. The following proportions
retain unmatched records within every observed journal/position group.

```{r}
#| label: cs04-fig-cs04-position
#| fig-cap: "Arbitrary lookup categories by recorded position in the synthetic fixture, including unmatched records. Empty positions have no observations."
#| fig-alt: "Faceted bars compare A, B and Unmatched shares by first, middle, last and single-author positions in two fictional journals."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
position_summary_example <- authors_example |>
  count(journal, position, lookup_category) |>
  group_by(journal, position) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(position_summary_example, aes(x = position, y = pct, fill = lookup_category)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  facet_wrap(~ journal) +
  scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = palette_sci(3), drop = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Recorded position", y = "Share of synthetic records", fill = "Lookup category") +
  theme_sci()
```

## Coverage by recorded year

The year comes from the fixture's explicit publication-year column, never from
an identifier. For each fictional journal/year, the denominator includes all
first- or single-author records. Each group has only one such record here, so
coverage is either zero or one. This illustrates denominator accounting; it
supplies no evidence about a demographic trend.

```{r}
#| label: cs04-fig-cs04-temporal
#| fig-cap: "Lookup coverage among first- or single-author records by explicit fixture year. Each fictional journal/year has one record; no demographic trend is measured."
#| fig-alt: "Lines show whether the one first-or-single-author record in each fictional journal/year matches an arbitrary lookup category."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
coverage_by_year <- authors_example |>
  filter(position %in% c("first", "single")) |>
  group_by(journal, year) |>
  summarise(records = n(), matched = sum(lookup_category != "Unmatched"),
            coverage = matched / records, .groups = "drop")

ggplot(coverage_by_year, aes(x = year, y = coverage, colour = journal)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2019:2021) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = palette_sci(2)) +
  labs(x = "Recorded fixture year", y = "Lookup coverage", colour = "Fictional journal") +
  theme_sci()
```

## What the fixture establishes

1. **Denominators change the result.** The fixture contains 15 authorship records:
   four A, four B and seven unmatched. Removing unmatched records would make A
   and B each half of the retained records, concealing that almost half of all
   records had no lookup match.
2. **Coverage differs by construction.** Example journal A has four matched
   records out of six; Example journal B has four out of nine. These differences
   follow from the invented name lists, not disciplinary or demographic evidence.
3. **Identity and contribution remain unobserved.** Neither the labels, the
   recorded positions nor their changes across fixture years support a claim
   about a gender gap, seniority or progress toward equity.

## Requirements for an actual study

<div class="callout callout-warn">
A real study needs a scientific question, a defined population and suitable
observations of the demographic variable of interest. Document their provenance,
ethical basis, categories, missingness and validation. Names cannot determine a
person's self-identified gender; a name-classification service, if used for a
carefully justified question, still needs context-specific validation and an
explicit account of what its labels measure. A confidence score alone does not
validate the resulting equity estimate. See Chapter \@ref(gender-limitations) and
[Santamaría and Mihaljević (2018)](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.156).

This fixture contains no demographic observations or real journal comparison.
No conclusion about a persistent gender gap, disciplinary differences or
temporal progress can be drawn from it.
</div>
